title: Index and ETF arbitrage
text: An ETF is a basket of stocks that trades as a single share. The share price and the value of the basket inside should match. When they drift apart, an arbitrageur trades one against the other, and that trade is what pulls them back together.

title: Create and redeem
text: The basket's value per share is the net asset value, or NAV. On the exchange, though, the ETF trades at whatever buyers and sellers agree. Authorized participants can deliver the basket to the fund and receive new ETF shares, or hand in shares and get the basket back. If the ETF trades at a premium, they buy the basket, create shares, and sell them. At a discount, they buy the shares, redeem them, and sell the basket. The SEC's ETF rule release, effective in December 2019, describes this as the mechanism that keeps market prices close to NAV.

title: The fast version
text: Most of the time, nobody waits for a creation. The SEC release cites an average of 90 percent of daily ETF activity on the secondary market. Fast traders watch every stock in the basket, compute a live fair value for the ETF, and quote or trade the ETF against the stocks, or against index futures. Creation and redemption are the slower valve, for clearing the inventory that builds up.

title: Index futures
text: Index arbitrage does the same between futures and the cash index. CME's fair value formula is the cash index, times one plus interest to expiry, minus the dividends paid before expiry. In CME's own example, the index is at 1,146, interest is 5.7 percent, there are 78 days left, and dividends are worth 3.47 points. That gives a fair value of 1,156.68. With futures at 1,157, they are 0.32 points rich. The arbitrage sells futures, buys the stocks, and holds until expiry, when the two must meet.

title: How it loses
text: The edge is the gap between two prices for the same thing. It loses through execution: hundreds of stocks must fill near the prices in the model, and a half-filled basket is an open position. In a fast market the fair value is stale before the orders arrive. Borrow costs, fees and wrong dividend estimates eat thin gaps. And many firms compute the same number, so the gap goes to whoever is fastest.

title: Building it
text: The lab has no ETF arbitrage yet, but it has the parts. Its book builder already rebuilds every Nasdaq order book from the ITCH feed, with prices as Price(4) integers. A fair value is a weighted sum of the constituents' mids. On each book update only one stock changes, so add its weight times the change in its mid, instead of re-summing the whole basket. That keeps the update constant time, however big the index.

title: Takeaway
text: Index and ETF arbitrage harvests gaps between a basket and its parts. It loses on legging, stale data and costs, so it belongs to whoever sees the whole basket first and fills it cleanly.
